case.display_title: Tired, off her food, with pain after meals

clock.day_0_label: Presentation to the out-patient department and admission (calendar date not reported)

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on anaemia in a 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and treated hypothyroidism, with two weeks of tiredness, poor appetite and pain after meals. We reviewed the Chart so far. If the reticulocyte count is raised, the marrow is responding, so this is not a simple failure of production; if the red cells are not microcytic and there is no history of bleeding, iron deficiency is unlikely. The possibilities include a haemolytic process, ineffective red cell production, and a toxic or nutritional cause. Treated hypothyroidism and diabetes do not explain an anaemia of this depth. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Ask for the blood film to be reviewed by a haematopathologist, looking specifically for red cell inclusions
LDH, haptoglobin and a direct antiglobulin test; iron studies, B12 and folate if not already done
Take a full medicine history, including herbal, traditional and over-the-counter remedies and supplements, current or recently stopped
No iron and no transfusion on current evidence while she is stable

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on anaemia; the Chart now includes coarse basophilic stippling. Coarse stippling with polychromasia and a reticulocytosis is an important finding: it points to a disturbance of haem synthesis or red cell maturation, a globin disorder or a red cell enzyme defect, and away from a nutritional cause. The iron indices, if high, fit a block in haem synthesis rather than iron deficiency. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Send a blood lead level
Send haemoglobin studies (HPLC)
Take a full medicine history, including herbal, traditional and over-the-counter remedies and supplements, current or recently stopped
A bone marrow is not needed before these results
Do not start iron

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on anaemia; the Chart now includes a blood lead of 121.2 ug/dL. This markedly raised level accounts for the anaemia, the coarse basophilic stippling and the reticulocytosis, and for any ring sideroblasts and dyserythropoiesis in the marrow, which are expected to resolve with treatment; they should not be labelled as a myelodysplastic process. Serum iron and ferritin are not low, so iron is not indicated. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Chelation under specialist guidance, once the source is identified and stopped
No iron: stores are replete
Full blood count and reticulocytes weekly during treatment
Repeat blood lead after the course and again for rebound
Cytogenetics only if the counts do not recover after treatment

consult_notes.note_text: Asked whether a toxic or environmental cause could explain abdominal pain after meals, poor appetite and anaemia in a woman with diabetes. We reviewed the Chart so far. Abdominal pain with an unexplained anaemia justifies a careful exposure history and targeted testing. No exposure is documented yet, so no specific toxic cause can be supported at present. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Take a detailed exposure history: a full medicine history, including herbal, traditional and over-the-counter remedies and supplements, current or recently stopped; occupation; hobbies; home and water supply
Send a venous blood lead level
Keep any product she has been taking, even if she has stopped it, in case it needs testing

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise; the Chart now includes a blood lead of 121.2 ug/dL. This level, in a symptomatic adult, warrants chelation. The source must be found and removed; Ayurvedic and other traditional remedies are a common source in India and should be stopped now. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Stop the suspected source before or alongside chelation
Chelation: parenteral dimercaprol (BAL) or calcium disodium EDTA at this level, followed by an oral agent (succimer, or d-penicillamine where succimer is not available)
Check full blood count, renal and liver function during the course
Repeat blood lead after the course and again two to three weeks later for rebound
Send the product to the drug analyst for testing, including for mercury and arsenic, and notify the drug regulator and public health

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on two weeks of abdominal pain after meals with poor appetite, anaemia and raised liver enzymes. We reviewed the Chart so far. There are no features of a surgical abdomen, and with no history of bleeding, blood loss is an unlikely cause of the anaemia. The transaminase rise has several possible causes, including viral hepatitis, fatty liver and drugs or remedies, which can injure the liver. Pain after meals with a soft abdomen and a normal ultrasound is unlikely to be primarily gastrointestinal. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Hepatitis B, C, A and E serology and a prothrombin time
Abdominal ultrasound if not already done
Endoscopy is not urgent; we would consider it for persistent dyspepsia, bleeding or iron deficiency
Review all medicines and remedies, including herbal products, as a cause of the liver tests
Consider metabolic and toxic causes of abdominal pain with anaemia

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on diabetes and thyroid disease in a woman admitted with anaemia and abdominal pain. We reviewed the Chart so far. Her diabetes is poorly controlled (HbA1c 9%) since she stopped metformin two months ago; with a reticulocytosis, the HbA1c may even underestimate her average glucose. Her hypothyroidism is controlled on thyroxine, and neither condition explains an anaemia of this depth. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Restart glucose-lowering treatment: metformin is suitable with her renal function
Capillary glucose monitoring while an inpatient
Take a full medicine history, including herbal, traditional and over-the-counter remedies, and ask why she stopped metformin
Continue thyroxine at the current dose
Check B12 periodically if metformin is restarted

accepted_differential: Other acquired sideroblastic anaemia (alcohol, drugs such as isoniazid, copper deficiency or zinc excess)
Haemolytic anaemia (reticulocytosis, mildly raised unconjugated bilirubin)
Arsenic or mercury toxicity from a traditional remedy
Nutritional deficiency anaemia (B12 or folate; tongue desquamation)

secondary_findings: Acquired sideroblastic anaemia from lead (ring sideroblasts), with a reticulocytosis

Poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9%) after stopping metformin
final_dx.text: Lead poisoning from an Ayurvedic herbal diabetes capsule bought online, presenting with abdominal pain, anorexia and fatigue, and anaemia with coarse basophilic stippling and ring sideroblasts

key_discriminators: coarse basophilic stippling on the film

must_do.text: Ask specifically about herbal, Ayurvedic or other traditional medicines and remedies bought online, especially for her diabetes
Have the peripheral blood film examined carefully for basophilic stippling
Stop the exposure (the capsules) before or alongside chelation
Chelate (symptomatic adult, blood lead about 121 ug/dL) with any appropriate chelator (dimercaprol, calcium disodium EDTA, d-penicillamine or succimer), with specialist advice
Send the product for analysis and report it to the drug regulator or public health
Restart effective treatment for her diabetes
Plan a repeat blood lead after chelation, because levels rebound

must_not_do.text: Label myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts before excluding reversible causes such as lead, alcohol, drugs and copper deficiency
Give iron therapy (serum iron and ferritin are not low)
Attribute the anaemia to diabetes or hypothyroidism without investigating it

ground_truth.outcome: Symptomatic improvement; haemoglobin 10.1 g/dL at discharge. After six weeks of d-penicillamine, blood and urine lead had fallen to normal and the film showed only a mild normocytic normochromic anaemia.
red_herrings: desquamation of the tongue and oral mucosa
high serum iron and transferrin saturation

rubric.text: Lead poisoning, with the herbal diabetes capsules identified as the source
Heavy-metal poisoning (including from a traditional remedy) without naming lead, poisoning by another metal, or toxic sideroblastic anaemia without naming lead
Myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts, haemolytic anaemia, thalassaemia trait, nutritional anaemia, acute porphyria or drug-induced liver injury as the final diagnosis
Unrelated diagnosis, or one that would lead to harm

teaching_points: Herbal and Ayurvedic remedies, including products sold online, can contain toxic amounts of lead
Patients may not volunteer remedies they have stopped or do not regard as medicines; ask specifically
Coarse basophilic stippling with ring sideroblasts points to lead before a marrow diagnosis of myelodysplasia
ground_truth.treatment_given: The herbal medicine was stopped. Chelation with dimercaprol (BAL), then oral d-penicillamine for six weeks. The capsules were sent to the state drug analyst (lead 40657.71 ppm against a permissible 10 ppm).

raw_material.findings: Normocytic normochromic anaemia. Coarse basophilic stippling of red cells. Normoblasts present. Polychromasia.
raw_material.note: The article says a 'careful examination' of the film revealed these features; the pathologist co-author examined it. Whether a routine first look missed the stippling is not stated. The film is taken as the admission sample (day 0).

The article's marrow report impression (an interpretation, not raw material): possible acquired sideroblastic anaemia from drug-induced lead or zinc poisoning, or possible myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts. Cellularity, dysplasia and karyotype not reported (gap G16).
Percentage of ring sideroblasts and iron stores not reported (gap G16).
raw_material.test: Bone marrow iron stain (Perls' Prussian blue)

raw_material.note: Undated in the article; reported in the Treatment section.

reports.impression: Normocytic normochromic anaemia with coarse basophilic stippling, polychromasia and normoblasts.
reports.report_text: Red cells are normocytic and normochromic. Coarse basophilic stippling is seen in a proportion of red cells. Polychromasia is present. Occasional normoblasts are seen. No spherocytes, target cells or red cell fragments. White cells are normal in number and morphology. Platelets are adequate in number.

reports.impression: Coarse basophilic stippling with polychromasia and normoblasts.
reports.report_text: Film reviewed by a haematopathologist. Red cells are normocytic and normochromic with coarse basophilic stippling in a proportion of cells, polychromasia and occasional normoblasts. No spherocytes, target cells or red cell fragments. White cells and platelets show no morphological abnormality. Comment: coarse basophilic stippling with polychromasia; suggest a blood lead level, haemoglobin studies and a detailed history of medicines and remedies.

Particulate, cellular aspirate. Marked erythroid hyperplasia, with a myeloid to erythroid ratio of about 1:2. Erythropoiesis is normoblastic with mild dyserythropoietic changes (occasional binucleate forms and nuclear budding). Granulopoiesis matures normally. Megakaryocytes are adequate with normal morphology. Blasts 1%. Plasma cells 2%. See the iron stain report.

reports.impression: Many ring sideroblasts; storage iron increased.
reports.report_text: Perls stain. Storage iron is increased (grade 4) in marrow fragments. Many ring sideroblasts are present, about 30% of erythroblasts. Comment: ring sideroblasts occur in acquired sideroblastic anaemia (toxins, drugs, alcohol, copper deficiency) and in myelodysplastic neoplasms. Suggest correlation with the history of medicines, remedies and exposures, a blood lead level, serum copper and cytogenetics.

reports.impression: Hypercellular marrow with erythroid hyperplasia; no infiltrate, excess blasts or fibrosis.
reports.report_text: Adequate trephine core. Cellularity about 60%, increased for age, with erythroid hyperplasia. Granulopoiesis and megakaryocytes are normal in number and morphology. No excess of blasts. No infiltrate, granulomas or fibrosis on reticulin stain.

reports.impression: No abnormal blast population; erythroid precursors increased.
reports.report_text: Bone marrow aspirate. CD34-positive blasts are under 2% with a normal phenotype; no abnormal blast population. Erythroid precursors are increased, in keeping with active erythropoiesis. Myeloid and monocytic maturation patterns are normal. Plasma cells are few and polyclonal.
Twenty metaphases analysed at a 400-band level. Karyotype 46,XX. No clonal abnormality detected.
Two hundred interphase nuclei scored per probe. Normal signal patterns for 5q31, 7q31, the chromosome 8 centromere and 20q12; no deletion or gain detected.

Targeted sequencing of a myeloid gene panel, including SF3B1, achieved adequate coverage across all regions. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were detected above the 2% variant allele frequency limit of detection.

The liver is normal in size and echotexture with no focal lesion. The gallbladder is thin-walled without calculi and the common bile duct is not dilated. The spleen measures 10 cm and is homogeneous. The pancreas, both kidneys and the aorta appear normal. No free fluid.

Supine abdominal radiograph. The bowel gas pattern is normal with no dilated loops. No abnormal calcification or radio-opaque material is seen. The visible bones and soft tissue outlines are unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis in the portal venous phase. The liver, spleen, pancreas, adrenal glands and kidneys are normal. The bowel is of normal calibre with no wall thickening. No lymph node enlargement, free fluid or free gas.

reports.impression: Mild non-specific antral gastritis. No ulcer or source of bleeding.
reports.report_text: Endoscopy to the second part of the duodenum. Normal oesophagus. Mild patchy erythema of the gastric antrum without erosions or ulceration. Normal duodenum. No varices or bleeding. Antral biopsies: mild non-specific chronic inflammation; no Helicobacter organisms.
Complete colonoscopy to the caecum with intubation of the terminal ileum; good bowel preparation. Normal mucosa throughout with no polyps, ulceration or source of bleeding.
